item.title: Three workers die at Tata Electronics' Hosur plant; Nalco Water confirms incident at utility facility
item.description: Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, on Tuesday confirmed that three workers employed by its subcontractor died in an incident at Tata Electronics' iPhone components manufacturing facility in Hosur, Tamil ...
item.content:encoded:
Three workers die at Tata Electronics' Hosur plant; Nalco Water confirms incident at utility facility Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, on Tuesday confirmed that three workers employed by its subcontractor died in an incident at Tata Electronics' iPhone components manufacturing facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, and said it was cooperating with local authorities investigating the deaths. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 16:11 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 16:11 IST

A security guard stands at the boundary of a Tata Electronics' components factory for Apple’s iPhone in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, India (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, on Tuesday confirmed that three workers employed by its subcontractor died in an incident at Tata Electronics' iPhone components manufacturing facility in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, and said it was cooperating with local authorities investigating the deaths. The company said the incident occurred at a utility facility operated by Nalco Water. "We are deeply saddened by the tragic incident that resulted in the deaths of three workers engaged by a sub-contractor of Nalco Water, an Ecolab company, at the Tata Electronics site in Hosur, India," the company said in a statement. "This incident occurred in a utility facility, operated by Nalco Water. We are working with the local authorities in the investigation of this incident," it added. The three workers died on Monday evening while carrying out maintenance work at an effluent treatment plant at Tata Electronics' Hosur facility, which manufactures components for Apple's iPhones. According to local authorities, the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank at the wastewater treatment facility. They were subsequently taken to a hospital, where they were declared dead, reported Reuters. Nalco Water said its immediate priority was to support the families of the deceased workers. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those impacted. Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected and our first priority is to extend all possible support to the families," the company said. Reiterating its commitment to workplace safety, Ecolab said, "Safety is a core value and is fundamental to everything we do at Ecolab. We take this incident extremely seriously." The deaths come amid growing scrutiny of Apple's manufacturing supply chain in India, which has emerged as a major production hub as the US technology company diversifies operations beyond China. India currently accounts for roughly 25 per cent of global iPhone production, with Tata Electronics contributing about 40 per cent of iPhone assembly in the country. Tata's Hosur operations have faced disruptions in the past, including a fire at its components factory in September 2024 that halted production. The facility also faced regulatory concerns over alleged water pollution earlier this year, although the matter was subsequently resolved. Separately, a ransomware attack affected an adjacent Tata Electronics iPhone manufacturing facility in Hosur earlier this year, exposing confidential company documents. (ANI)

item.title: China’s new Anti-Corruption law raises fears of legalising transnational repression, analysts say
item.description: China's newly enacted Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law has raised concerns that Beijing could use anti-corruption measures to legitimise its overseas operations against dissidents and political ...
item.content:encoded:
China’s new Anti-Corruption law raises fears of legalising transnational repression, analysts say China's newly enacted Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law has raised concerns that Beijing could use anti-corruption measures to legitimise its overseas operations against dissidents and political opponents, creating a chilling effect on critics of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), according to a report by The Epoch Times. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 15:58 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 15:58 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

China's newly enacted Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law has raised concerns that Beijing could use anti-corruption measures to legitimise its overseas operations against dissidents and political opponents, creating a chilling effect on critics of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), according to a report by The Epoch Times. The Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress (NPC) adopted the legislation on November 6, following the CCP's Fifth Plenum, which focused on advancing what the party described as "full and rigorous governance of the party" amid an expanding internal disciplinary campaign, The Epoch Times reported. According to the Chinese regime, the law formalises and consolidates operations by state agencies to track down and bring back Chinese nationals suspected of corruption who have fled overseas, while also enabling the confiscation of allegedly illegally acquired assets across international borders. However, analysts cited by The Epoch Times warned that the legislation could provide Beijing with a legal framework to expand its reach beyond China's borders and intensify pressure on overseas dissidents. Wang He, a US-based senior analyst, said the legislation was intended to provide the Chinese Communist Party with a legal basis to seek assistance and cooperation from Western governments while projecting an image of governance based on the rule of law. He noted that Western democracies generally lack extradition treaties with Beijing and frequently reject its requests for assistance in apprehending suspects because of concerns over China's lack of judicial transparency, political persecution of dissidents and religious believers, the death penalty, torture and other human rights violations. Wang Dan, a prominent Chinese dissident living in exile in Taiwan and a leader of the 1989 student democracy movement, also expressed concern over the legislation during his YouTube talk show. Describing the law as putting "on a legal cloak" for controversial overseas operations, Wang Dan warned that its broad coverage of alleged cross-border corruption could allow Chinese law enforcement agencies to expand their interpretation of jurisdiction. He said Chinese authorities could potentially scrutinise financial transactions between overseas dissidents and their relatives or associates in China, identifying individuals connected to such transactions as persons of interest in corruption investigations. This, he warned, could turn economic investigations into instruments of pressure and create a chilling effect among dissidents. Heng He, a US-based senior China analyst and current affairs commentator, told The Epoch Times that Beijing had previously faced international criticism for allegedly kidnapping or apprehending individuals overseas and was now seeking new legislation to legitimise such operations. He pointed to previous overseas "persuasion to return" campaigns, which allegedly involved stalking, threats and pressure on family members in China to compel targeted individuals to return. "Now, the new law will make it easier for Beijing to frame such actions as anti-corruption law enforcement," Heng said. Meanwhile, a Chinese lawyer identified by the pseudonym Zhang Ting, citing fears of reprisals, questioned the effectiveness of the legislation in addressing corruption within the country. He argued that corruption in China stemmed from the absence of effective checks and balances on political power and could not be resolved simply by introducing another law. Describing the legislation as "a tool for political purges", Zhang said it represented an extension of the CCP's internal power struggles. Wang, He further argued that the party's anti-corruption campaigns were selective and largely influenced by officials' political loyalty to top leadership. According to him, political alignments and factional rivalries within the CCP remained significant factors in determining who faced investigations and who received protection. He warned that when targeting political rivals, Beijing could mobilise a wider range of government agencies to trace financial assets and seek assistance from foreign governments. The new legislation, Wang He said, could consequently become a legalised instrument for political power struggles under the guise of anti-corruption enforcement. (ANI)

item.title: Japan's household spending falls 6.8% in September despite rise in income
item.description: Japan's household spending declined by 6.8 per cent in September 2026 compared to the same month last year, even as household income increased, according to official data released by the Statistics ...
item.content:encoded:
Japan's household spending falls 6.8% in September despite rise in income Japan's household spending declined by 6.8 per cent in September 2026 compared to the same month last year, even as household income increased, according to official data released by the Statistics Bureau of Japan on Tuesday. ANI | Updated: 10-11-2026 15:45 IST | Created: 10-11-2026 15:45 IST

Representative image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Japan's household spending declined by 6.8 per cent in September 2026 compared to the same month last year, even as household income increased, according to official data released by the Statistics Bureau of Japan on Tuesday. The latest Family Income and Expenditure Survey, released by Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, showed that average monthly consumption expenditure among households with two or more people stood at 289,536 yen (USD 1,833). The bureau said consumption expenditure was "down 4.5% in nominal terms and down 6.8% in real terms from the previous year." The decline marked the tenth consecutive month of falling household spending in real terms, indicating continued weakness in consumption. The fall in spending also deepened from August, when household expenditure had declined by 3.1 per cent year-on-year in real terms. On a month-on-month basis, household spending fell by 2.8 per cent in September after seasonal adjustment, compared with a marginal increase of 0.1 per cent in August. The detailed survey data showed that several major spending categories registered declines during September. Spending on education fell 23.5 per cent in real terms, while expenditure on transport and communication declined 9.1 per cent. Expenditure on fuel, light and water charges dropped 10.5 per cent, while spending on culture and recreation declined 8.7 per cent. Food expenditure also fell 2.5 per cent in real terms compared with September last year. However, household income increased during the month, contrasting with the decline in consumption. According to the survey, average monthly income among workers' households with two or more people stood at 528,074 yen (USD 3,343). The Statistics Bureau said household income was "up 3.4% in nominal terms and up 0.9% in real terms from the previous year." The figures showed that consumer spending continued to decline in September despite an improvement in inflation-adjusted income among workers' households. (ANI)
